vision_features.image_context: Close-up photograph of the underside or upper surface of a broad, dark green leaf. The leaf appears to be from a dicotyledonous plant, showing prominent veining and a hairy (pubescent) surface with fine white hairs visible along the edges and surface. The leaf is the sole plant organ visible.
vision_features.abnormalities: 1. Multiple discrete marks scattered across the entire leaf surface, distributed in both the left and right portions of the leaf. Each mark has: a dark brown to near-black central area (approximately 3–10 mm in diameter), an angular to irregular shape that often appears bounded or delimited by the leaf veins, and a bright yellow-to-yellow-green border or halo of 1–3 mm width surrounding the dark center. The dark central areas appear dry and somewhat sunken relative to the surrounding tissue. The yellow borders are vivid and distinct from the surrounding healthy dark green tissue. 2. In several locations, particularly along and adjacent to the main veins, the marks coalesce or are positioned so that multiple marks merge along vein boundaries, creating larger angular patches of dark brown tissue outlined in yellow. 3. The leaf margin in some areas shows dried, brown, curled tissue, suggesting the marks extend to the leaf edge in places. 4. The overall distribution is scattered but dense, with marks present across both halves of the leaf, ranging from small pinpoint-to-small (3–5 mm) to medium (8–12 mm) in size. No obvious pattern of concentration at the tip or base.
vision_features.absences: 1. No visible powdery or dusty coating on the surface of the marks or the surrounding leaf tissue. 2. No raised pustules, bumps, or thread-like outgrowths visible within or on top of the dark central areas. 3. No wet, slimy, or water-soaked appearance to the affected areas — the dark tissue appears dry. 4. No large-scale yellowing of the entire leaf blade beyond the immediate halos around individual marks.
vision_features.summary: The leaf displays numerous discrete marks scattered across its surface, each consisting of a dark brown to black dry center of angular to irregular shape, clearly bounded by the leaf veins, surrounded by a vivid bright yellow halo of 1–3 mm width. The marks range from approximately 3–12 mm and are present across the full leaf surface in high density. The leaf is the most severely affected organ visible. The most striking visual feature is the sharp, vivid yellow border contrasting with both the dark brown center and the surrounding healthy dark green tissue, combined with the angular vein-delimited shape of each mark.

Available classes in 'Soybean_Diseases' (5 total):

Knowledge-base entry for 'Bacterial_Blight':
────────────────────────────────────────
Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies. Lesions have dark reddish-brown centers surrounded by yellowish-green halos around water-soaked tissue; lesions may coalesce to form large, irregularly shaped lesions. Leaf veins may become affected creating necrotic areas resembling lightning on the leaf. Eventually lesions fall out leaving ragged foliage.. Presence of a yellowish-green halo around lesions; most common on young leaves in mid to upper canopy whereas brown spot is usually seen on older, lower leaves; lack of fungal structures in lesions.. Septoria brown spot, brown spot
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Diaporthe':
────────────────────────────────────────
Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped specks or pycnidia on mature soybean stems occurring later in the season (R6 to R8 growth stages). Pycnidia may also develop on dry, poorly developed pods, but may be dispersed randomly rather than arranged linearly.. Parallel rows of black, flask-shaped pycnidia arranged linearly on stems; random dispersal on pods.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phytophthora':
────────────────────────────────────────
Young plants show rapid yellowing and wilting with soft rot and collapse of the root. Mature plants exhibit general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, followed by wilting and death, with brown discolored roots and a dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes; leaves typically stay attached after plant death.. The best diagnostic symptom on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration (dark chocolate-brown) that may extend several nodes up the stem. Root system shows lateral and branch roots almost completely discolored; tap roots with brown surface discoloration and tan to brown inner tissue discoloration. Leaves turn yellow, wilt, and typically stay attached after plant death.. stem canker, Pythium
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phomopsis':
────────────────────────────────────────
Infected seed are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may have a gray mold on them.. Seed infected by pod and stem blight may decompose after harvest and have low viability; seedlings grown from infected seeds may often be blighted.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Green_stem_disorder':
────────────────────────────────────────
All or part of the soybean plant remains green while the rest of the plant or neighboring plants mature, most commonly seen in stems, leaves or pods; stems remain moist while pods and seeds have ripened.. Stems and occasionally leaves remain green and moist after pods and seeds have ripened and turned brown; excessive leaves on plant and green stems when neighboring plants are near harvest maturity.
────────────────────────────────────────

DISCRIMINATING: 'Bacterial_Blight' vs 'Phytophthora'
Ruling feature : Presence of angular leaf lesions with yellowish-green halos (Disease A) vs. dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending upward from the soil line with root rot (Disease B)
Bacterial_Blight: Bacterial Blight produces small, angular, water-soaked leaf spots with dark reddish-brown centers surrounded by yellowish-green halos, which may coalesce into irregular lesions and cause necrotic vein damage resembling lightning. Lesions eventually fall out leaving ragged foliage.
Phytophthora: Phytophthora causes dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration beginning below the soil line and extending several nodes upward, accompanied by brown/discolored roots and general yellowing of leaves progressing upward; leaves typically remain attached after plant death.
Decision rule  : IF angular leaf lesions with visible yellowish-green halos are present on upper canopy leaves, THEN suspect Bacterial Blight; IF dark chocolate-brown discoloration is observed on the lower stem at or below the soil line with root browning and leaves staying attached after wilting, THEN suspect Phytophthora.
